utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, Tuesday, the 6th of February, 2007, I'd like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, the Defence teams, the accused and everyone else in the courtroom. There are two oral decisions I would like to render very rapidly and then I'll give the floor to the registrar so that he can provide us with IC numbers. The first oral decision concerns the admission into evidence of documents presented through Witness CX. This witness appeared on the 22nd of January, 2006. The Chamber decides to admit the following documents presented by the Prosecution since they have a certain probative value and a certain pertinence. P 05554. I'll re-read that -- that's fine. P 08432 under seal. P 0895 [as interpreted] under seal, P 08898 under seal. There's an error. I'll reread that it's P 08895. 08895. P 09833. That is also under seal. P 08895 is also under seal. And then finally IC 00239. The second oral decision that concerns the documents related to the Witness DA who appeared on the 30th of January, 2007. The Chamber hereby decides to admit into evidence the following documents tendered by the Prosecution through the IC list, IC 00273, given that they have a certain probative value and a certain relevance. The Chamber would like to point out that the documents P 08157 and IC 00207 referred to in these lists are admitted under seal. In addition, the Chamber hereby decides to admit into evidence the following documents tendered by the Stojic and Praljak Defence teams. These documents are mentioned in the IC list, IC 00274, and in the IC list IC 00275, the reason being that these documents have a certain probative value and a certain relevance. The Chamber would also like to point out that document 2D 00339 referred to in the IC list 00274 is admitted under seal. The Chamber notes that the Prlic, Petkovic, Coric, and Pusic Defence teams have not requested that any other documents be admitted into evidence. I'll now turn to Mr. Mundis before the expert witness is called we have two other witnesses who hear, and I believe that one of them has requested protective measures, but first of all - I apologise, Mr. Mundis - the registrar also has some work to do able now give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. So two parties have submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness Damir Katica, and that's the OTP list, shall be IC 350, while the list submitted by 3D shall be given the Exhibit number IC 351. Again two parties have submitted list of documents to be tendered through Witness Munib Klaric. The OTP list shall be given Exhibit number IC 352, while the Defence 3D Defence list shall be given Exhibit number IC 353. Finally, there's also been a request, a list to -- list of exhibits to be tendered by OTP in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll deal with this matter later. Mr. Mundis, as I was saying, we have another two witnesses to hear. In order to save time, on behalf of my colleagues, but yesterday Judge Prandler clearly stated this, but what is important for us is to know what the nature of the wound is and where the shot was fired from. Everything else is of secondary importance. If you focus on these two elements, it will enable us to save time. Try to do your best because it is only on that basis that we, the Judges, will be able to rule. Mr. Mundis, you may have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. We appreciate the guidance from the Trial Chamber as always. The next witness will be taken by my colleague Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: As Your Honour has just pointed out, there is an application for protective measures with respect to this witness, somewhat unusually as there has been no written application as would normally be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should we move into -- let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Gillett, concerning the witness's profession, please avoid mentioning it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honour, for the purposes of the public record and a very abridged summary, given that this witness is called pursuant to Rule 92 ter, this witness in his statement gives evidence relating to sniping incidents in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Witness, do you remember being interviewed by somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor back in 2001?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And at that time did you answer the questions asked of you truthfully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was duty-bound to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you do so voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, at the end of that interview do you recall the statement being read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was read back to me. And I signed it even.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if the witness could be shown the B/C/S and English versions of his statement which are marked as Exhibit 9863.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see under the first tab of that bundle that's been given to you there are both an English and a B/C/S version of the statement. In due course I will be asking for this statement to be admitted under seal. Witness, if you could take a look at the statement and confirm whether or not that is your signature or initials on each of the pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to read this statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Gillett. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Gillett. I would like to only ask one question -- or, rather, a correction in the witness's statement, because you just referred to it. Since I'm not supposed to mention his profession, I would like to say that in the fourth paragraph of his written statement, both in the English and the B/C/S version, probably there is a problem, fourth paragraph, that he volunteered in a certain year, 1959, and later on he became a professional one. But on the other hand, of course, at that time he was only seven years -- pardon. So it is only what I would like to ask for a correction here, because he was very young then according to this statement. If you see my point, that he couldn't be a volunteer in that very year because of his age. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to ask the witness whether or not he has any additions or corrections to make to the statement, and perhaps for these purposes it might be prudent to pass briefly into closed -- private session in order that I can ask him about the date concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, prior to coming into court today or indeed yesterday, have you had the opportunity to re-read your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And having re-read the statement, is there anything in that statement that you wish to withdraw or to correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing. I stand by my statement, what I said in 2001, and what I signed I say now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. In due course the Prosecution will be tendering this, as I mentioned, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mention on the second page of your statement a person whose name I won't mention in open session in order not to identify you, a person who was killed on the -- back in 1994, and you mention where you were when you saw this, and once again I won't mention that in open session. What I want to ask you to clarify is at the time when you saw this, how far away were you from the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, roughly I would say between 12 and 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And was there anything obstructing your vision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm trying to speed up and save time. In your written statement you tell us of four events, but actually in the -- of the four you only saw something happen in one of them. All the rest is hearsay. So what we're interested in is what you saw, and what you saw was on the 2nd of March, 1994, and you were 12 metres from where the person fell. We already heard witnesses about that. Now, what I am interested in is this: From where you were, did you see where the shot came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will deal with that matter straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, in 2004 did you meet with an investigator and a photographer of the ICTY in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, at that time were you asked a series of questions that were relating to the incident that His Honour the Judge has just mentioned and that is mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We carried out a reconstruction of the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall was this question and answer session videotaped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two video cameras taping and one or two others.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Perhaps we can pass into private session because I'm going to ask if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I'm going to give the floor to the registrar who has two numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. In relation to the OTP response to the list of documents tendered by the 3D through Witness Dzevad Hadzizukic. The exhibit will be -- become 369. There is another list provided by OTP in response to the lives documents tendered by the 3D Witness Munib Klaric which will become IC 370.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we've the next witness shown in I'd like to turn to Mr. Mundis. For the expert witness tomorrow, Mr. Mundis, as you know we made an oral decision on the duration and we told you, you would have two hours and the Defence would have four hours. Since we're under great time constraints and are running late, as the Presiding Judge and having the job of directing the proceedings, I think that it is relevant and useful for the good of one and all to say that when embarking on your examination-in-chief you should not take it in the American way but in a more efficacious way and that the examination-in-chief should start off by asking the expert witness or, rather, with respect to the CV of the witness that can be done very quickly and then to tell us what material was at the base of his report. He -- that he went on location, that he met with the investigator, that he took photographs, et cetera, et cetera, to explain to us how he prepared all that. And then a third stage that he makes a brief expose of the weapons used by snipers, by sniper X. That's already in his report, of course, but he can tell us what type of weapon was most probably used and that he could give us a brief expose on calibre, the calibres of the bullets. That's also in his report, so he can do that too. And after that you could ask him perhaps to comment on all the incidents that he mentions and deals with in his report, the first case, second case, third case, et cetera, that we can place maps established by him incidents by incidents on the overhead projector which he can explain to us. For case number 1 he drew incident, positioning the victim, the direction, the trajectory, supposed trajectory of the projectile, and so on, so he can comment the sketch drawn by him for each individual case, and then he can say that in his opinion the shot came from 600 or whatever metres under such-and-such an angle and so on. And by asking precise, specific questions and by hearing the comments of the expert witness, we will have a vision of the work done by the expert. And then the Defence, within the four hours at their disposal, will have ample time to go back if they deem necessary on any specific points. Now, as we've already heard the victims, we Judges already have all the facts of the problem, and we shall intervene with questions to the witness, because what is important for us is to know where the shots came from. So having said that, Mr. Mundis, think about it all in the interests of time and being as efficacious as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just two very brief comments. It -- what you've outlined is virtually identical with the play plan that we will use with the expert tomorrow, so I think we're certainly on the right track there. And I would hate to take all the credit for the American style and, of course, we stole that from the British. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, we'll see whether the British style is efficacious. We'll test that tomorrow. So there we have it. Let's have the next witness shown in, and once again we'll try and get through the proceedings as rapidly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not the only thing they stole, Your Honour. Would they give us the language back sometime as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Mundis agrees with you, Mr. Stewart, there. If there's no answer, then I think that will mean agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On this occasion, the silence can be taken to mean agreement. I will reserve in other situations, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Since we're all making jokes, if everyone were to give back to everybody else what they had taken from them in the first place, everybody would be left with very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, good evening. I assume you can hear me. Can you give me your name, surname, and date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Enes Vukotic. I was born on the 10th of August, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an economist, a retired economist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, have you ever testified in a court of law before or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified in a court of law, although I have made statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would you now go ahead and read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of explanations. From me you are going to start off answering questions put by the Prosecution. They will also probably be showing you some documents. And after that it will be the turn of the Defence. They will be asking you questions within the cross-examination. And the Judges might also ask you questions, if they deem necessary. The object of your coming here is to testify about the shots that took place in the town of Mostar, so it is within that framework that you are going to give your contribution and testimony. So without further ado, I give the floor to the Prosecution for a brief summary of the basic points of your written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good evening to Your Honours, Mr. President, to everybody else in the courtroom. I'll now proceed with the brief summary which was drawn from the 65 ter statements. In this case the witness lived in Donja Mahala and Mostar and was a -- I'll change this to a member of the Territorial Defence and later joined the ABiH army. On the 13th of May, 1993, the witness left home around 4.00 to 5.00 p.m. He was not wearing any military clothing. His neighbour was with him. They got to the pedestrian bridge which goes from Donja Mahala to the area of Luka. The witness was aware that there were snipers shooting at people on the bridge from the houses on the hill called Stotina. They would shoot at anyone including women and children. When they got to the bridge, some people there actually warned them to take care because the bridge was being shot at. His neighbour ran across the bridge and made it into the alley on the other side without being shot at. When the witness saw he was safe, he ran across the bridge, turned left, and then stopped near the entrance of the alleyway close to a container behind which police officers were hiding. The witness stopped for about 30 seconds and was hit in the leg above the right knee. He was taken to the hygienic institution and stayed in the hospital for two days. And that would conclude the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Vukotic. Did you provide written statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on the 3rd of September, 2001?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but, yes, I did make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at that time you provided this written statement did you answer the questions of the investigator fully and truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, certain, truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you do so freely and without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of that interview was your statement read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage with the assistance of Madam Usher, I wonder if the witness could be presented with a bundle of exhibits which includes his statement, which is Exhibit 09864. Now, I'll mention to Your Honours that that is name in this statement that I'd prefer not to have made public and for that reason perhaps the statement could be under seal or, alternatively, perhaps Your Honour would wish to make an order redacting the name in the statement. It's the name of his neighbour, and I just want to mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to place it under seal. That will be simpler. So, Mr. Registrar, the number 9864 exhibit will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just know the reason why the name's not to be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I just wouldn't like to mention this person's name given the recent ruckus that occurred in Mostar. He might be somewhat afraid if his name were mentioned in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not good enough. We have lots and lots of names mentioned here. I have no wish to cause any trouble for any particular gentleman but it's simply not good enough. It's entirely speculative whether there's any problem, and we have names mentioned lots and lots of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any difficulties or likely to be any difficulties but given we didn't have the consent of this person, I thought it prudent not to mention his name. However, if the Court rules otherwise, so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The name is the name of the person who crossed the bridge first; is that right? Is that the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, you're going to contact this person, are you, to hear his position? And if he has nothing against it, we can lift the seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I can do that, if Your Honour wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, could you look at the first exhibit on 9864. This shows an English and Bosnian statement given to the ICTY. Could you in particular look at the English version, and you'll see some signatures at the end. Is it correct that this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall that you met with an investigator and myself yesterday morning when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at that meeting do you remember that I asked you whether you had -- whether or not you had re-read your statement and whether you wanted to make any corrections to your statement, and is it correct to say that you had no corrections to make?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I read my statement. I completely agree with it, and I don't think there's any need to add or subtract anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember that you mentioned some additional information to us?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. Could you remind me? I don't know what you mean, what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you -- I'll ask you very few questions for the benefit of the Court to expound on that purpose. In your statement on page 2 you said you knew there were snipers shooting at people on the bridge, and they were in Stotina.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I knew that. But up until that day they were shooting people walking by on the pedestrian bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting, sir, but just to be quite clear on about what you're saying, you were a member of the BH army. Can you tell us what unit you belonged to the day you were fired at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was a member of the 1st Company of the 2nd Battalion of Donja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the name of the commander of the 1st Company and of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite frank, they would change frequently. The company commanders would change frequently, so I really done remember who was the commander at that time. But if necessary, let me stress that I am a member -- was a member of the Territorial Defence, and I became a member in June 1992 of the Territorial Defence when the war with the Serbs began. I was there for a short time and was then dismissed along with some other people of my own age, and the reason given for my dismissal was logistics, that the army or logistics didn't have enough resources, didn't have food to feed us all, nor did they have enough ammunition, weapons, and cigarettes. And so we were told that the army didn't need us any more and they let us go. But when the war with the Croats started, and that was on the 9th of May, 1993, officially, I was asked to return to help out and to be a guard, if nothing else. Now, who the commander was at that point in time I really can't say. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a follow-up question. You were, therefore, a member of the 2nd Battalion. Now, the 2nd Battalion, what area of activity was that in, area of operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The defence of this part of Mostar, Donja Mahala, where I lived, and standing guard -- doing guard duty at the Bulevar and Podvelezje. That was more or less the general location and what our company was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for specifying. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just on that subject, Mr. Vukotic, could you just for the assistance of Their Honours indicate if you had a uniform as a member of the ABiH? Were you provided with a uniform?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank there weren't enough to go round. Not ammunition, or weapons, and especially uniforms. So I didn't have a uniform at all. I wore civilian clothes when I went to do my guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in your statement, on the critical day, the 13th of May, you said you were dressed in civilian clothes. Could you tell Your Honours what colour those clothes were, and if you could describe them.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was wearing jeans, faded jeans, they were old jeans, and I had trainers on my feet, and my upper half, well, I had a jacket of some kind and a T-shirt. Light clothing. That was intentional, so I could move around or run across the bridge faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you also said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Running across the bridge. Did you have a weapon that was apparent, visible, or was it hidden on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I had absolutely nothing on me, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you on duty at the time you crossed the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I wasn't on duty. Unfortunately, I was forced to go to hospital to fetch medicines for my daughter who had been wounded three days before that by a shell, the shrapnel of a shell. So I had to cross to the opposite bank of the Neretva to go to the hospital and get the medicines for her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, sir. I've been told of an event. If you don't feel well at any point in time, please don't hesitate to let us know and we can take a break. Do you understand, sir? Any time you're feeling unwell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can continue. That was just a moment, a moment of weakness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, I know that you're not to be stressed. Sometimes questions can be very stressing -- stressful. So I would like to ask everybody to take note of that, to bear it if mind. If you don't feel well, don't hesitate to let me know, because your evidence is important but your health seems to me to be more important. So please do not hesitate. If at any time you're having problems, tell us and we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, but I think I'm ready to continue now that I've calmed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor, I have a question following up from what the President has just said. Your friend and neighbour, Witness - we won't mention the name - who was with you, was he a military man? When you were with him at that time, what was he wearing? Was he wearing military clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was last member of the BH army. What his assignment was at that particular time I really don't remember. And I think, although I can't claim, but I don't think he was wearing a military uniform, although I am not sure. But I don't think he was, because we crossed the Neretva on private business. Where he was going I can't remember, but I think -- I can't claim, but I don't think he was wearing military uniform, precisely because he was afraid of snipers while crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did he have a visible weapon on him or a weapon that he had hidden on his person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. As I say, we were getting ready to run across, so I can say that quite definitely, that he did not have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, as far as is possible, without giving -- don't give the name of your neighbour. So avoid naming your neighbour in future. Mr. Flynn, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And just again for the assistance of the Court, you described in your statement that the weather was just nice that day. Could you perhaps elaborate on it? Would you say it was a sunny day or just a normal day, or could -- perhaps you could elaborate on it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was sunny or not, but that it was a nice day, that's certain. I judge that by the way I was dressed. So it was a clear day, if I can put that way. It was May in Mostar, but whether it was sunny or not I can't say, but it was certainly warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And going back to the question I earlier -- I asked you -- I started to ask you earlier, you mentioned the houses on the hill called Stotina where there were snipers shooting at people. Can you tell us who was occupying those houses? What group of people, organisation, or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: The HVO was organised first, at the beginning the war. I claim that, and I claim that Hum or, rather, Stotina, was held by the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, again in your statement you said that people warned you about snipers. Did you meet anybody before you crossed the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: We did know. We had information that that pedestrian bridge was specifically targeted and part of Donja Mahala, I don't know how far your are acquainted with the situation in Donja Mahala, or, rather, the plateau, Stotina is up above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your answer leads me to a question that I absolutely have to ask. You said in your written statement, and you just confirmed it, that in -- at Stotina there were snipers. Now, even if you're running, theoretically speaking a good sniper has enough time to hit his target. So what made you cross the bridge and run the risk of being hit by a bullet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. I was forced to go and fetch medicines for my daughter because she had been wounded by the shrapnel of a shell on the 10th of May, and -- well, you're quite right. It was -- the bridge is rather wide, but to our advantage was the fact that the bridge had concrete pillars somewhere in the middle. So in running across we could take shelter or hide behind these concrete pillars, wait a few seconds and then run to the next pillar and cross the bridge that way, avoiding being hit by the sniper. So there were these concrete pillars at every four or six metres that held up the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We Judges were in Mostar, and I can't actually say whether I saw the bridge or not, nor that I recall the pillars, but a question comes to mind. Wouldn't it have been wiser to cross the bridge at night? Unless, of course, a sniper had night vision sights. But apart from that, wouldn't it have been wiser to cross the bridge at night rather than in daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps that was my mistake. Perhaps I wasn't thinking straight, or perhaps my neighbour convinced me to go earlier. Perhaps you're right. Maybe it would have been better to go at night. I acknowledge that I made a mistake there. But was that a reason for him to shoot me, hit me? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's another problem. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I wonder with the permission of the Court, I haven't included it in the bundle, but this often-used map, if I may put it to the witness, with the assistance of Madam Usher, just to orient ourselves. If you could put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukotic, I'm going to show you a map, and if you take a pen, have a look at the map, and you will see on the map the area Luka and Donja Mahala. If you could just draw with a pen where you think the bridge was.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to find my way on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you see the river?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I see the river, but to locate the pedestrian bridge which is no longer there, it doesn't exist any more, that's difficult. But roughly, I suppose, it would be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps this might assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Again with the permission of the Court because I got it this morning and I didn't include it in the bundle. It's a wider picture of the screen shot of the general bank of the river. Again if I could put it on the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I think your house may have been somewhere over to the left of that photograph. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Can you see these two buildings which we call the Sokol buildings? My house is there, between the main road and these two highrises. That's where my house is located, and I assume that over here is where -- well, the bridge isn't there any more so it's difficult for me to find my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you estimate where the bridge might have been using these two large brick buildings or square buildings?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, it's roughly here or here, slightly northward. These might be the pillars, the remaining pillars on the banks of the Neretva. I think those are the pillars, and, yes, that's the playground. If you see these two pillars on the banks of the Neretva, I think they are the remaining pillars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Place a cross there, please, where the bridge was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. And your house. Can you indicate where your house was?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: It should be somewhere here. Maybe it's here in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mark the bridge with number 1 and your house with number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And lastly, before we leave the photograph, you mentioned these houses on Stotina. Using the river as a reference, could you look at the photograph and could you circle the houses in Stotina where the snipers were sniping from, if it's on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't think you can see it. They should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the houses on the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. I seldom go up there, though there are a lot of new buildings that have been constructed there. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell us where the -- in crossing the bridge, if you were to walk across the bridge from Mahala to Luka where Stotina would have been? Would it have been on your left, your right, behind you?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think it's here in front of me. I think this is where the plateau is, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you put a circle on it, please, for me, and the number 3.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: But there's one thing I'm not clear about. There's a street here that leads to the aluminum company. I can't see it. That's the street. That's the street here. So Stotina is here. I've found my bearings now. This is the street that leads to the aluminum company and Stotina and the plateau should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If you could just mark a circle where you imagine it would be or where you think it would be, even if it's off the map.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think it's here.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your initials on the document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will become Exhibit number IC 371.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vukotic, do you remember that in 2004 you met an investigator from the ICTY, Mr. Spork, and a photographer from the Tribunal at the location where the shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I remember meeting a certain gentleman. I really can't remember what his name is. I also remember the date, because at the time at his request I obtained a certificate that concerned me having been wounded. That's why I remember the year. But I really can't remember the name of the gentleman. I gave a statement, and he accompanied me to the site of the event, and we reconstructed the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And he asked you a number of questions. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that was event videotaped?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I think it was videotaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At this stage I wonder if the witness could be shown -- with the assistance of the case manager, if the witness could be shown video P 01490 on Sanction. The sound isn't great on the video so the transcript is attached to the bundle of documents and it's transcript number 1. We're ready to start the video if you're in Sanction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Ms. Winner says it doesn't seem to be working. [Videotape played]. "Investigator: Mr. Vukotic, could you please indicate the location of the former bridge that you were crossing on the day that you were shot?"

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Are Your Honours getting a picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have a picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It seems that we have technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours. What I'll do is I'll move on for the moment and I'll come back to it. Perhaps we can rectify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Apart from the video, Mr. Vukotic, do you remember that the -- can you tell us whether the photographer took a number of photographs, still photographs, at the same time when you met?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I didn't quite hear you question clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: My question was: Apart from making the video, do you remember if the photographer took a number of still photographs while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can just show him the photographs. We'll concede the fact that the photographs were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Karnavas always has excellent ideas. Mr. Flynn, show him the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps we can show him the photographs on 09139, exhibit 09139, the 360-degree photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sir, you remember we did this yesterday. Do you see -- do you see a photograph in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I can see myself at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It seems we have another problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, if we have a hard copy it would be best to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. It's working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you have a photograph in front of you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It's gone again, Your Honours. Now we see it; now we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph is fixed, apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on my screen. Well, yes, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you remember when we looked at these yesterday, Mr. Vukotic, a melange of 360-degree photographs? Could you do the same now, and at the conclusion I'd like you to tell us if you can the direction in which you believe the shot came from, and also the position of the police post that you mention in your statement. If you want to, just say stop.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Stop here. I'd just like to point something out. I think -- or, rather, it's more that I'm persuaded of the fact. I think that this was subsequently built and this wall wasn't here before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. And if we continue on to the right. Did you say stop?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No, no. Let's continue. Stop. This is the beginning of the street or, rather, this is the corner, the angle of the wall where I stopped for a minute to have a rest. I leaned against the wall at the beginning of this small street.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which direction you were facing?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: With my back to the south or, rather, to Stotina and the bridge, and my face -- or, rather, I was facing this small street.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If we could just continue to the right, and tell me if you see where your back was fasting.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'll repeat what I said. I was leaning against the edge of this wall. The greenery here wasn't there before. This is an abandoned area. That's where I was. I don't know if there's anything else I should add.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll go into Sanction, Your Honours because it will make a lot more sense if we watch the video and then watch the 360.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So I'm going to go back to the video and counter of the meeting you had with the investigators, and if you could watch this carefully for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: "Investigator: Mr. Vukotic could you please indicate the former bridge that you were crossing on the day that you were shot? "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Mr. Vukotic, could you please indicate to the best of your recollection where you were standing when you were shot? "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Mr. Vukotic, could you please indicate where the police was hiding behind? "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Mr. Vukotic, to the best of your recollection could you please indicate the position you were in when you were shot? "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Could you please indicate where the bullet hitter body? "Witness: [Indicates] "Investigator: Mr. Vukotic, was the pole situated on the location of the [inaudible] at the time when you were shot? "Witness: [Interpretation] No. "Investigator: Thank you very much. I will mark a yellow X on the spot where the witness was standing when he was hit."

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you recognise yourself in the video?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a little younger then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And on the video when you were asked about where the bullet hit you, you showed your right leg, and you were pointing to your right leg, somewhere around the knee, and you pointed to the front of your leg just above the nowhere the bullet came out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you were leaning over slightly as you were talking, according to the video -- from your recollection on the video, you were leaning over as you were talking to the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was leaning against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you hear any shot accompanying the bullet that struck you?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't think I heard the shot. And even if I had heard it, well, I don't know. Other shots were fired earlier on. Other -- later on even if this shot had been intended to for me, I doubt that I would have had time to take shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we take the angle at which you were standing at when you were shot, if you were to turn around 180 degrees, can you tell us the direction which you would have been facing?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd be facing Stotina. I don't know if that's your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That's exactly my question. And was there anything -- did -- could you have a clear view of Stotina, and was there anything to your knowledge blocking the view Stotina would have of you?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I quite naively thought that they were only monitoring the pedestrian bridge. If I had got a foot into the street I would have been safe, but I was naive. So it's my fault as far as that is concerned. I thought snipers were monitoring the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When we were looking at the 360 photographs a few moments ago, you made reference to this view, and I'd like to present it to you to be put on the ELMO if it's possible. It's an excerpt from 09139, Exhibit 09139. This pole, did this pole exist there? Was it there at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No. Had the pole been there, I would have been sheltered. The pole wasn't there. This was an open space. This pole was subsequently placed there. Unfortunately, people used all the timber they could find for heating, so they would cut such things down. But I don't think the pole was there at the time. It was subsequently placed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the greenery we see to the left of the pole, did that exist?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Similarly, as what I have said, this has grown there because it hasn't been used for years. You can't even see the Neretva River because of all the greenery.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Again when we were looking at the 360 photos, we saw an alleyway and I believe this was the alleyway you were about to turn into and there was a police post. Can I hand you another screen shot, which is a screen shot of the alleyway, and tell me, is there anywhere on this photograph that the police post was constructed, or was it off the photograph? Where do you remember the post being?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that this building opposite the spot at which I was standing was subsequently built. The container [as interpreted] was here more or less and the police were in -- somewhere in the street. I don't even think the steps were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you mark, please, where you think the police post was? Could you put an X.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Somewhere here more or less where you can see the new wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were the policemen standing out in the open to be seen, and could they be seen from the Stotina direction?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No, certainly not. They couldn't have noticed anything because of this wall that's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the last question, Mr. Vukotic, base on your own knowledge of events at the time and what you yourself could observe and what you were told by other people about the presence of snipers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. I'm not interested in what he was told. What his knowledge is, fine. What he observed, fine. But what he was told later is hearsay and is unhelpful in trying to determine from which direction this gentleman was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm actually referring to what he was told before he crossed the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges where you believe the shot came from? That is, the location of where the shot came from. Bearing in mind all of those elements.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: My claim is that the shot could have only come from Stotina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was there any -- was there shooting on that day from any other part of the other side of the bank of the river?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: No shots could have come from the other side of the river because the right bank was under the control of the ABiH and Stotina was under HVO control. So the shot could have only come from Stotina and from nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I said the last question. This is truly the last question. I think yesterday you gave to us a number of medical reports that you obtained from the medical authorities in Mostar which make reference to your injury, isn't that correct? Sustained on this day.

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think those medical reports make reference to a bone -- a bone injury to your right leg in addition to a flesh wound. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, when I was wounded, I was taken to an institute which was the only one that functioned as a military hospital on the left bank, but then they were unable to determine bone fracture because they didn't have the appropriate X-ray device. So they just used an ordinary bandage to bandage my leg. And two days later I asked them to discharge me because the bandage was of no help to me. I said someone could do that at home. An ordinary nurse could bandage my leg. And the hospital was full of the wounded, and I thought it was useless for me to take up a bed. So I asked them to send me back home two days later. And then at night I was returned there. We acted a little more intelligently then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn that you had sustained more than just a flesh wound to your leg?

utterances.speaker: ENES VUKOTIC
utterances.text: Later, several months later, after a few check-ups, I don't know the right medical terms but I had a complication on that part of my knee. So on two or three occasions I went to the hygiene institute to have it treated. And then they obtained the X-ray device, and they discovered that the bone had been fractured but it healed as it healed. But my leg is worse and worse every day. It's shorter, about two centimetres shorter than it was, and all because the appropriate treatment wasn't provided. And the conditions were such that it wasn't possible to provide such treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a question I'd like to put to you. We'll check this, because we have all the documents on admission to the institute of hygiene, so we can see whether you were on the list, but your knee was hit by a bullet according to what you have said. Your bone was fractured. Did the bullet pass through your knee or was the bullet extracted from you at the institute of hygiene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an entry and exit wound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the bullet didn't remain in your leg. It probably ended up in the wall, on the ground. It passed through you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea. I couldn't know about this at the time, but it's quite certain that the wound was an entry and -- that it was an entry and exit wound. That's all they determined. The bullet wasn't found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you'd been provided with the treatment, when your wound had been disinfected, when the leg had been bandaged, the entry wound was large and the exit wound was small or was the reverse the case? As far as you can remember, what was the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember. I wasn't able to observe the state of my leg. I paid no attention to it. I didn't know anything about these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But usually when one is hit in the leg one pays attention, but you say you don't remember. Did you lose a lot of blood or not much blood? Were there stains on your trousers or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The trouser had been stained but not soaked. It hurt a lot. It hurt a lot when I tried to reach shelter in the street. I saw the blood. I didn't have the strength to look. I fell down, and my neighbour who was there -- there was a vehicle on duty because of such cases, because of that sniper on the bridge, so I was fortunate because I was immediately transported the to the institute of hygiene. There was this vehicle on standby. But as to how much blood there was, well, there was blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 6, page 113 says there was a vehicle on standby. I thought there were lawyers on standby but now there are vehicles on standby. So now you're telling us there was a vehicle permanently at the site in order to assist the wounded. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that I was fortunate because at that point in time there was a vehicle that was ready for such cases at Titova Street. I was fortunate because at that point in time the vehicle was there and I was immediately transported to the institute of hygiene. As to whether it was there all the time or whether it changed the location, I don't know. But when I was wounded they immediately put me into the vehicle and took me to the institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have two brief questions that I would like to put to you very briefly. You spoke about a police post which was near the spot where you were wounded, and on the day that you were wounded there were many other shots. There had been many other shots prior to your wounding. Were there any shots that were fired from the police post in the other direction? Was there an exchange of fire, in other words? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Answer the first question first, please. Did the police at the police post own fire on Stotina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, those policemen, I know that from before and later on, those policemen were put there on the right bank of the Neretva. There were two civilians. And where I crossed there were two policemen. Whether they were the classical type of policemen or not I don't know, but they were wearing uniforms. That I do know. And they had the task of providing security for the bridge or, rather, to control and take the -- look at the identity cards of people crossing the bridge, because it was in fashion -- it was fashionable at the time to blow up bridges. So they were the ones that checked the ID cards of people who they did not know approaching the bridge. Now, whether they shot later on or not, I don't know. Their task was just to control the access to the bridge to unknown persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, my second question, second to last question, is this: In the hospital there were a lot of wounded people. Were there as many civilians as military men or were they mostly civilians? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really can't answer that. I can't claim either way. I didn't follow those things, but I think that there were more civilians. I would say that there were more civilians. My neighbours -- I don't know whether you're acquainted with Mostar, where Mahala is and the northern districts. There were people older than me who were wounded by shrapnel from shells, and I would say there were actually more civilians at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll see that on the basis of the records we have. Another question from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will wait for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague prefers asking his question tomorrow. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good evening, Witness. For us to be able to be ready tomorrow and not ask superfluous questions, it is important for us to know the direction -- or, rather, how the -- the direction of the entry/exit wound, where the bullet entered and where it exited, because without that we can't establish anything. So the possible direction in respect of the river and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few seconds. We see your leg and your knee. Now, the bullet, did it enter on the right-hand side or the left-hand side of your leg, and where did it exit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd prefer it if some professional were to look at this. I can't see to the back of my leg to see the exit wound. You can see the entry wound very easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have the impression that you're not asking my -- answering my question frankly. It's a simple question. You were wounded. You said there was an entry wound and an exit wound. So my question is very clear. Where was the entry wound? Was it to the right or to the left of your knee? For an economist, I'm sure you understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question, but let me repeat that at this point in time, well, I didn't give it much thought. I don't remember, nor did I look at the wound in recent years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't then. I'm not asking you about then. I'm asking you about now, today. You must know where the bullet entered, unless your knee is in perfect condition without any more traces of the wounding. And then you can say no, you don't know. But you said that you -- your leg was two centimetres shorter, and yet you're unable to tell us where the bullet entered your leg. It's important for us to know the position, because on the basis of the position of the wound we can establish the direction the shot came from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I'm sorry. I really can't answer that. I can show you. I can show you the exit wound, but I really can't show you the entry wound. I feel very uncomfortable now, but I really can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Take a look at your knee between now and tomorrow morning and perhaps you can tell us tomorrow whether it was on the left or on the right. Mr. Flynn, do I take it that you have completed your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes. I omitted to just -- to ask you formally -- or to mention formally that I would be tendering the statement that I had summarised earlier in evidence. But apart from that, I have no further questions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we reconvene tomorrow morning. My colleague the Judge will be asking you a question, and if you can tell us where the entry wound was that will be useful. If not, well, do the best we can. It is 10 minutes past 7.00. I apologise for the delay and for keeping you all longer. We had to do that, but we reconvene tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of February, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.10 p.m.,
